v: Read Norwegian out loud without guessing
Handle æ, ø and å
Say your first ten words

b.v: Norway has two written standards. This course teaches Bokmål, which about nine out of ten Norwegians write. Spoken Norwegian has many dialects, but everyone understands the kind you will learn here.

v: æ = like the a in cat (være = to be)
ø = like the u in burn, with rounded lips (øl = beer)
å = like the aw in law (år = year)

b.v: They come at the very end of the alphabet: … x, y, z, æ, ø, å. Dictionaries and phone contacts sort them there too.
2) Letters that sound different from English

v: j = y as in yes (ja = yes, jeg = I, said 'yai')
y = a tight ee with rounded lips, like German ü (by = town)
u = between oo and ee (du = you)
kj = a soft hiss, close to the h in huge (kjøkken = kitchen)
sk before i, y, ei, øy = sh (ski = 'shee')
skj = sh (skjorte = shirt)
rs = sh in most of eastern Norway (norsk = 'nosh-k')

b.v: Do not say jeg as 'jeg' with a hard j. It is 'yai'. It is the word you will say most often.

v: d is often silent at the end: god (good) = 'goo'
g is silent in -ig: hyggelig (nice) = 'hyg-ge-li'
h is silent before v and j: hva (what) = 'va', hjem (home) = 'yem'
t is silent in det (it) = 'deh' and in the -et ending
ja = yes
nei = no
hei = hi
takk = thank you
unnskyld = excuse me / sorry
vann = water
kaffe = coffee
hus = house
bok = book
venn = friend

b.v: Read these aloud, slowly, then faster.|ja – nei – hei – takk|jeg – hva – hjem – god|ski – kjøkken – norsk|være – øl – år

v: Greet at any time of day
Thank people the Norwegian way
Say goodbye correctly
Hei = hi (works with everyone, everywhere)
Hallo = hello (also on the phone)
God morgen = good morning
God dag = good day (formal, less common now)
God kveld = good evening
God natt = good night (only when going to bed)

b.v: Norwegian has a formal 'you' (De), but almost nobody uses it any more. You say du to your boss, a shopkeeper and the prime minister. This is normal, not rude.

v: Hvordan har du det? = how are you?
Bra, takk. Og du? = fine, thanks. And you?
Det går bra = it's going well
Ikke så verst = not too bad

b.v: 3) Thank you – Norwegians say it a lot

v: Takk = thanks
Tusen takk = thanks a lot (literally 'a thousand thanks')
Takk for sist = thanks for last time (said when you meet someone again)
Takk for maten = thanks for the food (say it after every meal you are served)
Vær så god = here you are / please help yourself / you're welcome
Ingen årsak = no problem

b.v: There is no everyday word for 'please'. Politeness comes from the way you ask: Kan jeg få …? = can I have …?

v: Ha det = bye
Ha det bra = goodbye (take care)
Vi ses = see you
Vi snakkes = talk soon
Ha en fin dag = have a nice day

b.v: Say this conversation out loud twice.|Hei! Hvordan har du det?|Bra, takk. Og du?|Det går bra. Takk for sist!|Ha det bra!|Ha det!

v: Say your name, where you are from and where you live
Ask the same of someone else
Meet the verb å være (to be)
Jeg heter Khalid = my name is Khalid (literally 'I am called')
Hva heter du? = what is your name?
Hyggelig å treffe deg = nice to meet you
I like måte = likewise
Jeg kommer fra Pakistan = I come from Pakistan
Hvor kommer du fra? = where do you come from?
Jeg er pakistansk = I am Pakistani
Jeg bor i Oslo = I live in Oslo
Hvor bor du? = where do you live?

b.v: Nationalities and languages are written with a small letter: norsk, engelsk, urdu, pakistansk.
3) å være – the easiest 'to be' in Europe
Norwegian verbs do not change for the person. 'Am, is, are' are all er.

v: jeg er = I am
du er = you are
han / hun er = he / she is
vi er = we are
dere er = you (all) are
de er = they are
Jeg snakker urdu og engelsk = I speak Urdu and English
Jeg snakker litt norsk = I speak a little Norwegian
Snakker du engelsk? = do you speak English?
Jeg er lærer / ingeniør / student = I am a teacher / engineer / student

b.v: No 'a' before a job: Jeg er lærer, not Jeg er en lærer.
Introduce yourself out loud.|Hei! Jeg heter …|Jeg kommer fra …, men jeg bor i …|Jeg snakker … og litt norsk.|Hva heter du?

v: Know the three genders
Say 'the' the Norwegian way – as an ending
Make simple plurals
en = masculine: en bil (a car), en venn (a friend)
ei = feminine: ei bok (a book), ei jente (a girl)
et = neuter: et hus (a house), et eple (an apple)

b.v: In Bokmål every ei-word may also take en: en bok is correct too. So in practice you learn two groups: en-words and et-words.
Norwegian does not put a separate word for 'the' in front. It adds an ending.

v: en bil → bilen = the car
en venn → vennen = the friend
ei bok → boka (or boken) = the book
et hus → huset = the house
et eple → eplet = the apple
en bil → biler (cars) → bilene (the cars)
en venn → venner → vennene
et eple → epler → eplene
short et-words often do not change: et hus → hus (houses) → husene (the houses)

b.v: 4) Learn the word with its gender
Always learn a new noun as a pair: en stol (chair), et bord (table), en dør (door), et vindu (window). The gender decides the ending, so it is worth the effort.
Say 'the …' for each word.|en kopp → koppen|et glass → glasset|en telefon → telefonen|et rom → rommet

v: Count to a hundred
Say prices in kroner
Give your phone number
null, en (ett), to, tre, fire, fem
seks, sju (or syv), åtte, ni, ti
elleve, tolv
tretten, fjorten, femten, seksten
sytten, atten, nitten, tjue
tjue (20), tretti (30), førti (40), femti (50)
seksti (60), sytti (70), åtti (80), nitti (90), hundre (100)
21 = tjueen, 35 = trettifem, 99 = nittini
200 = to hundre, 1 000 = tusen

b.v: Unlike German, Norwegian counts the tens first, like English: 45 = førtifem (forty-five).

v: The money is the krone (kr). 1 krone = 100 øre, but øre coins are gone.
Hva koster det? = what does it cost?
Det koster nittini kroner = it costs 99 kroner
Det blir to hundre kroner = that comes to 200 kroner
Norwegians pay by card or with the Vipps app almost everywhere.

b.v: Norwegian mobile numbers have eight digits and are usually read in pairs: 41 23 45 67 = førtien tjuetre førtifem sekstisju.
Read these aloud.|17 – 70 – 18 – 80|kr 49 – kr 120 – kr 999|Telefonnummeret mitt er …

v: Use any verb in the present
Ask yes/no questions
Say 'not' in the right place

b.v: Most present-tense verbs end in -r, and that form is the same for every person. This is the best news in the whole course.

v: å snakke → jeg snakker, du snakker, vi snakker (speak)
å spise → spiser (eat)
å drikke → drikker (drink)
å bo → bor (live)
å jobbe → jobber (work)
å forstå → forstår (understand)
å ha → har (have)
å gå → går (go/walk)
å komme → kommer (come)
å like → liker (like)
Du snakker norsk. → Snakker du norsk? = do you speak Norwegian?
Han bor i Bergen. → Bor han i Bergen?
Question words come first: Hva spiser du? Hvor bor du? Når kommer du?
hva = what
hvor = where
når = when
hvem = who
hvorfor = why
hvordan = how
Jeg forstår ikke = I don't understand
Jeg snakker ikke tysk = I don't speak German
Liker du ikke kaffe? = don't you like coffee?

b.v: The verb always stays in second place. If a sentence starts with a time word, the subject moves after the verb: I dag jobber jeg (today I work) – not I dag jeg jobber.
Make each sentence a question, then a 'not' sentence.|Du liker te. → Liker du te? → Du liker ikke te.|Hun jobber i dag.|Vi forstår norsk.

v: Order in a café
Name everyday food
Pay and ask for the bill
Kan jeg få en kaffe? = can I have a coffee?
Jeg vil gjerne ha … = I would like …
En kopp te, takk = a cup of tea, please
Har dere …? = do you have …?
Hva anbefaler du? = what do you recommend?
brød = bread, smør = butter, ost = cheese, egg = egg
melk = milk, vann = water, juice = juice, te = tea
kylling = chicken, fisk = fish, laks = salmon, ris = rice
grønnsaker = vegetables, frukt = fruit, eple = apple
Er dette halal? = is this halal?  Uten svinekjøtt = without pork
Kan jeg betale? = can I pay?
Regningen, takk = the bill, please
Kan jeg betale med kort? = can I pay by card?
Kvittering = receipt
Det var godt! = that was good!

b.v: Tipping is not expected in Norway. Rounding up for good service is enough.

v: Hvor finner jeg …? = where do I find …?
Det er for dyrt = it is too expensive
Har du en pose? = do you have a bag?
Ja, takk / Nei, takk

b.v: Order a meal out loud.|Hei! Kan jeg få en kylling med ris?|Og et glass vann, takk.|… Det var godt! Kan jeg betale med kort?|Takk for maten!

v: Ask the way and understand the answer
Use bus, tram and train words
Buy a ticket
Unnskyld, hvor er …? = excuse me, where is …?
… togstasjonen = the train station
… bussholdeplassen = the bus stop
… sykehuset = the hospital
… toalettet = the toilet
Er det langt? = is it far?
til høyre = to the right
til venstre = to the left
rett fram = straight ahead
ved siden av = next to
over gata = across the street
Det er fem minutter å gå = it is a five-minute walk
buss = bus, trikk = tram, T-bane = metro (Oslo), tog = train
fly = plane, ferje = ferry, taxi = taxi
billett = ticket
Når går neste buss til sentrum? = when does the next bus to the centre leave?

b.v: In most cities you buy tickets in an app (for example Ruter in Oslo). Riding without a valid ticket gives a large fine.

v: En billett til Bergen, takk = one ticket to Bergen, please
Enkeltbillett = single ticket
Tur-retur = return
Hvilket spor? = which platform?

b.v: Ask the way to the station out loud.|Unnskyld, hvor er togstasjonen?|Gå rett fram, så til venstre.|Er det langt?|Nei, det er ti minutter å gå.|Tusen takk!

day-9.t: Day 9 — Days, time and the weather

v: Say the days and months
Tell the time – including the tricky 'half'
Talk about the weather
mandag, tirsdag, onsdag, torsdag, fredag, lørdag, søndag
januar, februar, mars, april, mai, juni, juli, august, september, oktober, november, desember
i dag = today, i morgen = tomorrow, i går = yesterday
helg = weekend
Hva er klokka? = what time is it?
Klokka er tre = it is three o'clock
kvart over tre = quarter past three (3:15)
kvart på tre = quarter to three (2:45)
ti over tre = 3:10
fem på tre = 2:55

b.v: halv tre means 2:30, not 3:30. Norwegians say 'half to three'. This catches almost every learner.
Timetables and shops use the 24-hour clock: 14.30 = halv tre in the afternoon.

v: Hvordan er været? = how is the weather?
Det er sol = it is sunny
Det regner = it is raining
Det snør = it is snowing
Det er kaldt / varmt = it is cold / warm
Det blåser = it is windy
Det er minus ti grader = it is minus ten degrees

b.v: Norwegians say: Det finnes ikke dårlig vær, bare dårlige klær – there is no bad weather, only bad clothes.
Answer out loud.|Hva er klokka nå?|Hvilken dag er det i dag?|Hvordan er været i dag?

v: Hold a short conversation
Review the whole course
Know what comes next

Hvor kommer du fra?|B: Jeg kommer fra Pakistan, men jeg bor i Oslo nå.|A: Snakker du norsk?|B: Litt. Jeg lærer norsk hver dag.|A: Så bra! Vil du ha en kaffe?|B: Ja, gjerne. Tusen takk!

v: jeg is said 'yai'
du is fine for everyone
Kan jeg få …? instead of 'please'
Takk for maten after a meal
en / ei / et, and 'the' goes on the end: bilen, huset
